It's played on ice, and the object of the game is for two teams to push heavy stones across the ice towards a target. Now, there are four people in each of the two teams. The first is called the lead. The next is called the second. The next, surprise surprise, is called the third. And unlike ice hockey ice, for example, it is constantly groomed by frequent shaving to keep it perfectly level. At either end of this are the two zones for the targets. Each one is known as a house. But then it was decided to add a handle to get a better grip. The other distinctive implement is the brush, or broom. This is used for two purposes: to clean the ice, of course, but more crucially, to warm it. This melts the ice slightly and lessens the friction, so you get a smoother slide. parts.transcript: Hello everyone. I recently completed some important research into the way office space is designed and its impact on employees. The open-plan office had been the norm for offices around the world. I'm sure you can picture one: a big room with maybe 50 or 100 workers sitting at their workstations. You might think open-plan designs are a recent phenomenon, but they actually came about in the early 20th century when businesses needed large numbers of people to do typing. These employees, usually women, used to have to sit in rows working away at their typewriters under the watchful eye of their supervisor. Over the years, designers have come up with several variations on the open theme. In particular, this has been achieved through furnishings. The early designs featured separate desks. A subsequent design introduced the concept of the cubicle. These can have either high screens that workers can't see over, or a screen just low enough to keep a lookout for the manager. And nowadays, with the increase in large call centers, a phenomenon known as hot desking is common. In this system, employees working on different shifts are asked to share the same workstation. As you can imagine, this is not very popular with staff, as there is little opportunity to personalize your workspace. In fact, my research shows that employees in general dislike the open-plan design. As a part of my research, I conducted a survey of the staff in several large companies with open-plan offices. The employees all voiced similar concerns about the design. Firstly, they felt that the open-plan took away their privacy. But many also felt the need to carry their valuables with them at all times. So to some extent, they also felt there was less security with these designs. Another common complaint may be something for employers to consider when choosing this type of design, and this was that these types of office space are bad for the health. I was intrigued by this possibility, but looking at staff records, it does seem to be borne out. So if this design is so unpopular, why is it so commonplace? Well, the answer to that is in the benefits that the employers feel this type of design has. Of course, there is the obvious benefit that this design significantly reduces costs, both in terms of rent and even in terms of energy use. Employers also argue that an open-plan design leads to better teamwork and communication. They also feel that new staff can learn from observing other workers, so this design can actually help in training staff. However, the complaints voiced by employees seem to suggest that the disadvantages far outweigh the advantages. The reality is that unhappy workers are unlikely to work well together, and there is plenty of evidence to suggest workers are frequently distracted from their work by the noise that is all around them. What is clear is that, as designers, we need to think carefully about the impact that our design has both on the staff involved and the work that they do.

task1.title: Task 1: Formal / Semi-formal Letter
task1.prompt: You recently stayed at a hotel on an official business trip and encountered several problems during your stay. Write a formal letter to the hotel manager. In your letter: explain why you were staying at the hotel, describe the problems you experienced, and state what actions you expect the manager to take.
task1.sampleBand8Answer:
Dear Sir or Madam,

I am writing to formally register my disappointment regarding the quality of accommodation during my stay at the Grand Imperial Hotel from October 18th to October 21st (Booking Reference: #GI-98421). I was visiting your city as the keynote speaker at the International Energy Symposium.

Regrettably, multiple deficiencies compromised what ought to have been a restful business visit. First, despite confirming a high-floor executive quiet room weeks prior, I was assigned Room 204 adjacent to the main loading dock, where delivery freight commenced noisily at 5:00 AM each morning. Furthermore, the high-speed Wi-Fi connection advertised in the executive suite failed intermittently throughout my stay, preventing me from accessing critical presentation materials for my conference.

To compound these issues, when I raised these urgent concerns with the front desk duty supervisor on the morning of October 19th, the staff member appeared dismissive and failed to offer an alternative room or technical support.

In light of these inconveniences and the substandard service rendered, I request a refund of 50% of the total accommodation fee charged to my corporate card. Additionally, I would appreciate a written assurance detailing the measures you intend to institute to improve staff responsiveness and internet stability.

I look forward to receiving your prompt resolution.

Yours faithfully,
Dr. Jonathan Miller

task2.title: Task 2: General Essay
task2.prompt: In many countries today, people are spending less time with their families and more time at work or pursuing individual hobbies. What are the causes of this trend, and what effects does it have on society?
task2.sampleBand8Answer:
In contemporary society, an increasing number of individuals devote an overwhelming proportion of their daily lives to workplace commitments and autonomous pastimes, resulting in a noticeable decline in familial interaction. This essay will examine the primary catalysts behind this phenomenon and discuss its profound ramifications for community cohesion.

The primary impetus behind diminishing family time is escalating economic pressure and the competitive nature of the globalized job market. With housing costs and general living expenses soaring in metropolitan hubs, adults frequently find themselves obliged to work excessive overtime or manage secondary freelance gigs to attain financial stability. Concurrently, the pervasive presence of personalized digital entertainment—such as algorithmic social media and on-demand streaming—encourages solitary engagement rather than collective domestic pastimes.

Regarding the impacts, this societal transition generates considerable adverse repercussions. Within the household, the lack of parental presence and meaningful communication can weaken intergenerational bonding, leaving children vulnerable to behavioral issues and emotional isolation. At a broader societal level, the erosion of cohesive family structures diminishes the collective resilience of communities, as strong domestic units have traditionally served as the initial safety net during psychological and financial crises.

In summary, intense corporate demands and digital individualism represent the chief reasons why people are drifting from domestic life. Unless societies institute sustainable work-life balance policies, familial ties and social well-being will continue to erode.

part2.title: Part 2: Individual Long Turn / Cue Card (3-4 mins)

cueCard.prompt: Describe a memorable professional or academic achievement that you are proud of.
bullets: When and where it took place
What challenges you had to overcome
And explain why you felt so proud of this accomplishment.

part2.sampleBand8Answer:
I would like to speak about a defining professional achievement from last year, when I successfully spearheaded the migration of our company's legacy customer management infrastructure to a secure cloud platform. This undertaking occurred over a grueling six-month period at our regional corporate headquarters.

The primary obstacle we confronted was the sheer complexity of legacy data formats, compounded by an unforgiving deployment deadline. We had to ensure zero downtime for over fifty thousand active global clients while synchronizing disparate legacy databases. Furthermore, midway through the project, several senior specialists had to quarantine due to seasonal health issues, which forced me to shoulder additional architectural duties and coordinate with offshore teams across multiple time zones.

Ultimately, the migration went live seamlessly without a single minute of service disruption. I felt immensely proud not only because the project cut infrastructure overhead by thirty percent, but because it substantiated my leadership capabilities under immense pressure and earned our team formal recognition from executive leadership.
